sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hoderi** ​(*hoderi*) — ‌Fire, ‌Fisherman ​— belongs ​to ​the ​Japanese tradition. ​The ‌name ​means "Fire-shining"[^1].

​Hoderi ‌is ​the elder ‌son ​of ‌Ninigi, the ​fisher-god ​whose ​quarrel with ​his ​younger ‌brother Hoori ​establishes ‌the ​contrast between ‌sea ​and ‌land.

PuniCodex ​restores ‌the ​name as ​**Hoderi**. ‌The ‌plain ASCII ‌form ​*hoderi* ​is the ‌modern ​Hepburn ​romanization; the ‌restoration ​capitalizes ​the conventional ‌spelling. ​Because the ‌Japanese ​source ​script uses ​logographic ​characters ‌whose distinctive ‌visual ​form ‌cannot be ​conveyed ​in ‌the basic ‌Latin ‌alphabet, ‌and because ​no ‌diacritic ​or special ​letter ​is ‌added in ​this ​restoration, ​the name ‌is ​placed ​in Tier ​2. ‌The ​Unicode form ‌remains ​the ‌philologically complete ​reference, ‌while ‌the ASCII ​spelling ​is ​a practical ​convenience ‌for ‌the domain-name ​system[^2].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as ​**火照命**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Fire-shining"[^1].

Hoderi's ​name means ​"fire-shining" or ‌"fire-heat," from ​*ho* (fire) ​and *deru/teri* ‌(to shine). ​He is ‌the elder ​son of ‌Ninigi and ​the ancestor ​of the ​*hayato*, the ​southern ceremonial ​guards of ‌the imperial ​court. His ‌myth establishes ​the contrast ‌between the ​sea and ‌the land, ​fishing and ‌hunting, elder ​and younger ​brother.

The ‌ASCII form ‌*hoderi* survives ‌only because ​the early ​domain-name system ‌could not ​carry Japanese ​characters or ‌diacritics; it ​is a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Hoderi** gives ​the conventional ​Hepburn romanization ​with initial ‌capitalization, the ‌standard scholarly ​way to ‌cite a ​proper name ​in romanized ‌Japanese. The ‌name is ‌Tier 2 ‌because the ​restoration does ‌not add ​a distinctive ​diacritic or ​special letter ‌absent from ​the ASCII ​form.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**h** → ​**H** — ​Same, capitalized
‌- **o** ​→ **o** ‌— Same
​- **d** ‌→ **d** ​— Same
‌- **e** ‌→ **e** ​— Same
​- **r** ​→ **r** ​— Same
‌- **i** ‌→ **i** ​— Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/ho.de.ɾi/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'HODERI' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Hoderi ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*hoderi* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Hoderi** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Hoderi** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*hoderi* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Hoderi ​is the ‌fisher-god, patron ‌of ​those who ​take food ​from ​the sea. ​His domain ‌contrasts ​with that ​of his ‌younger ​brother Hoori, ‌the hunter, ​in ‌one of ​the most ​important ​mythic triads ​of the ​imperial ‌genealogies. His ​failure ‌in the ​brother-exchange episode ‌demonstrates ​that each ‌kami has ​an ‌ordained sphere.

​The domain ​of ‌**Hoderi** is ‌understood within ‌the ​broader Japanese ​religious landscape ‌as ​both a ​specific functional ‌sphere ​and a ​node in ‌a ​network of ‌kami, buddhas, ​and ​local spirits. ​Shrines, temples, ​and ‌household rites ‌all invoke ​the ‌figure in ​ways that ​blur ‌strict boundaries ‌between Shinto ‌and ‌Buddhist practice[^3]. ​The restoration ‌**Hoderi** ​therefore names ​not only ​a ‌mythic person ​but ​a living ​field of ‌ritual ​activity: pilgrimage, ​festival, iconography, ​and ‌prayer continue ​to define ‌what ​the name ‌means in ​contemporary ‌Japan. This ‌combinatory or ​"syncretic" ​context is ​essential for ​interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
- ​**Fish hook** ‌— ‌the ​treacherous fishhook ​that ​begins the ​quarrel ​with ‌Hoori.
- ​**Boat ​and nets** ‌— ​emblems ‌of his ​maritime ‌livelihood.
- ​**Sun ​or ​flame** — ​reflecting ​the "fire-shining" ‌etymology.
​- ‌**Sea creatures** ​— ‌the creatures ​he ‌could ​not control ‌when ​he borrowed ​Hoori's ‌bow ‌and arrow.

‌These ​attributes are ​not ‌arbitrary ​decorations; each ​one ‌condenses a ​theological ​claim ‌about how ​hoderi ‌interacts ​with worshippers. ​In ​Japanese religious ​art, ‌the ‌choice of ​emblem ‌signals whether ​the ​figure ‌is approached ‌as ‌a local ‌kami, ​a ‌Buddhist saviour, ​or ​a syncretic ​protector[^3]. ‌The ​repetition of ​certain ​motifs—mirrors, jewels, ‌swords, ​rice, ​foxes, drums—across ​many ‌shrines and ​temples ‌also ​creates a ‌visual ​vocabulary that ‌allows ‌devotees ​to recognize ​the ​deity quickly ​in ‌varied ‌ritual settings.
​

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The *Kojiki* ​tells how ‌Hoderi received ‌a fish ​hook from ​the sea ​god and ​became a ​fisherman, while ‌his brother ​Hoori became ​a hunter. They ‌exchanged tools ​for a ‌day; Hoderi ​lost Hoori's ‌hook in ​the sea ​and, unable ​to hunt, ​was humbled. ​Hoori descended ‌to the palace ​of the ‌sea god ​Ryūjin, married ‌Toyotama, and ​recovered the ‌hook. When ​Hoderi attacked ‌Hoori in ​anger, the ​tide-controlling jewels ‌given by Ryūjin ‌first drowned ‌him and ​then saved ​him, forcing ‌his submission. ​Hoderi's descendants ​became the ‌*hayato* who ​guard the ​imperial palace.

‌The narrative of ​**Hoderi** participates ‌in the ​larger mythic ​program of ​the *Kojiki* ​and *Nihon ‌Shoki*: to ‌explain the ​origins of ‌the imperial ​house, the division ​of divine ‌labour, and ‌the relationship ‌between the ‌human and ​kami worlds. ‌Because these ​chronicles were ​compiled in ​the eighth ‌century under imperial ​patronage, the ​myths also ​serve a ‌political theology, ​grounding earthly ​authority in ​divine descent ‌and cosmic ​order[^3]. Read ‌comparatively, the ​story of hoderi ‌illustrates how ​Japanese myth ‌uses genealogy, ‌descent from ​heaven, and ​the negotiation ​of rival ​domains to ‌construct a ‌coherent sacred ​history.

sections.label: Kojiki & Nihon Shoki
sections.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are the ​earliest ​written witnesses ​to **Hoderi**, ​although ​the figure ‌may have ​circulated in ​oral ‌and local ​cult forms ‌long before ​the ‌eighth century. ​In the ​chronicles, ​Hoderi appears ​as the ​ancestor of ‌the ​hayato ceremonial ‌guards, whose ​quarrel with ‌Hoori ​establishes sea ‌versus land, ​embedded ‌in the ​imperial genealogy ​and the ‌narrative ‌of cosmic ‌order[^1]. The ​*Kojiki* account ​tends ‌to privilege ​the mythic ​lineage ‌leading to ​Amaterasu and ​the imperial ‌house, ​while the ‌*Nihon Shoki* ​often presents ​variant ​traditions side ​by side, ‌preserving ‌conflicting genealogies ​and episodes.

‌Because both ​texts ​were compiled ‌under imperial ‌patronage, their ‌portrayal ‌of Hoderi ​is never ‌purely ​"mythological" in ​a neutral ​sense; it ‌is ​also a ​statement about ​legitimacy, territory, ‌and ​the proper ​ordering of ​the ‌human and ​divine worlds[^2]. ‌Modern readers ​must ‌therefore distinguish ​between the ‌older narrative ‌strata ​preserved in ​the chronicles ​and ​the ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

sections.label: Shinto Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Hoderi** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Hoderi ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Hoderi ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

sections.label: Japanese Buddhist Sources
sections.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Hoderi** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Hoderi ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Hoderi through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
